Bosnian Church
BOZ-nee-an church
proper noun (a medieval church body)
From Bosnia; the independent medieval church of Bosnia, of disputed character, sometimes linked to the dualist Bogomil heresy, flourishing roughly from the twelfth to the fifteenth century.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Bosnian Church was an independent medieval church body in the kingdom of Bosnia, flourishing roughly from the twelfth to the fifteenth century, standing apart from both Rome and Constantinople, and of much-disputed character. Some historians have linked it to the dualist Bogomil heresy—a movement akin to the Cathars, teaching two eternal principles of good and evil, an evil material creation, and a docetic Christ—while others judge it to have been a schismatic but broadly orthodox monastic church with peculiar customs. The historical evidence is fragmentary, and the dictionary treats the question with due caution, neither asserting more than the sources warrant nor passing over the doctrinal issue at stake. What the dictionary will name plainly is the error of dualism, if the Bogomil link be granted. Dualism, in any form, is a corruption of the biblical doctrine of creation: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth; by Christ were all things created, visible and invisible; every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused; and God saw everything that He had made, and it was very good. There are not two eternal principles, but one God who made all things, and a creation good in its origin though fallen by sin. To make matter evil in itself is to deny the goodness of the Creator and the reality of the incarnation, in which the Son took true flesh. The dictionary marks the Bosnian Church as a sober case-study: a church cut off from the wider body and from the full light of Scripture drifted into obscurity and, perhaps, into heresy, and under Ottoman conquest its people largely passed into Islam. The lesson it teaches is the danger of a Christianity severed from the Word and the catholic faith, and the abiding truth that the one God made all things good.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An independent medieval church of Bosnia (12th-15th c.), apart from Rome and Constantinople, of disputed character—possibly linked to the dualist Bogomil heresy; a case-study in the danger of a church cut off from Scripture and the catholic faith.

BOSNIAN CHURCH, proper noun. An independent medieval church of Bosnia, 12th-15th century.

It stood apart from both Rome and Constantinople.

Of disputed character, sometimes linked to the dualist Bogomil heresy.

Dualism is a corruption of creation: one God made all things good (Genesis 1:1; Colossians 1:16).

Its people largely passed into Islam under Ottoman conquest.

📖 Key Scripture

Ge 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Col 1:16 — "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:"

1 Ti 4:4 — "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:"

Ge 1:31 — "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

If the Bogomil link be granted, the Bosnian Church carried the dualist heresy—two eternal principles, an evil material creation, a docetic Christ—a corruption of the doctrine that one God made all things good.

expand to see more

The dictionary treats the disputed character of the Bosnian Church with due caution, for the historical evidence is fragmentary and scholars differ on whether it was a dualist Bogomil body or a schismatic but broadly orthodox monastic church with peculiar customs. The dictionary will not assert more than the sources warrant. But the doctrinal issue, if the Bogomil link be granted, is grave and worth naming. Dualism teaches two eternal principles of good and evil, an evil material world made by a lesser or evil power, and a Christ who only seemed to take flesh. This is a fundamental corruption of the faith.

Against all dualism the dictionary sets the plain word of Scripture: in the beginning the one God created the heaven and the earth; by Christ were all things created, visible and invisible; every creature of God is good; and God saw everything He had made, and it was very good. There are not two eternal principles but one Creator, and the creation is good in its origin, marred only by the sin that entered it. To call matter evil is to slander the Creator and to deny the incarnation, in which the Son took real human flesh. The Bosnian Church, whatever its precise doctrine, stands as a sober case-study of a Christianity cut off from the wider body and the full light of Scripture, drifting into obscurity and, under Ottoman conquest, largely into Islam—a warning of the danger of a church severed from the Word and the catholic faith.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Bosnia; the Crkva bosanska (“Bosnian Church”), an independent medieval body; possibly linked to the Bogomils, the Balkan dualist sect kin to the Cathars.

expand to see more

Crkva bosanska, “the Bosnian Church,” the independent medieval body.

Stood apart from both the Roman and the Eastern churches.

The Bogomils, a Balkan dualist sect, to whom it is sometimes linked.

Dualism: two eternal principles, an evil material creation, a docetic Christ.

Largely absorbed into Islam under Ottoman rule after the fifteenth century.

Usage

"He named dualism as a corruption of creation, set against the one God who made all things good."

"She saw in the Bosnian Church a warning of a Christianity cut off from Scripture and the catholic faith."
